content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published guidelines addressing mental health in the workplace, emphasizing the critical relationship between mental health and work. Mental health is not merely the absence of mental health conditions but rather a state of well-being that enables individuals to manage life’s stresses, realize their abilities, learn effectively, work productively, and contribute to their communities. Mental health conditions can arise regardless of whether work has directly contributed to them. Poor mental health negatively impacts cognitive, behavioral, emotional, social, and relational well-being, as well as physical health, personal identity, and work-related functioning. This can lead to reduced productivity, impaired performance, unsafe work practices, and challenges in retaining or gaining employment. The economic and societal costs of poor mental health are significant, with presenteeism (reduced productivity while at work), absenteeism, and staff turnover affecting both workers and employers. It is estimated that 15% of working-age adults have a mental health disorder at any given time. Despite the magnitude of this public health issue, investment in addressing mental health conditions remains insufficient, even though international conventions advocate for the protection of workers’ physical and mental health through national occupational safety and health policies. The WHO guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations for promoting mental health and preventing mental health conditions in the workplace. These include organizational interventions, training for managers and workers, and individual-level interventions. The guidelines also address strategies for supporting individuals returning to work after an absence due to mental health conditions and for helping those with mental health conditions gain employment. Key Recommendations: 1. Manager Training for Mental Health Support: Managers of health, humanitarian, and emergency workers should receive training to enhance their knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors regarding mental health. This training aims to improve their ability to support the mental health of their teams effectively. 2. Mental Health Literacy and Awareness Training: Health, humanitarian, and emergency workers should be trained in mental health literacy and awareness to improve their understanding of mental health issues and reduce stigmatizing attitudes in the workplace. 3. Universal Individual Interventions: Psychosocial interventions, such as mindfulness-based or cognitive-behavioral approaches, can be universally delivered to workers to build stress management skills, promote positive mental health, reduce emotional distress, and enhance work effectiveness. Opportunities for leisure-based physical activities, such as resistance training, strength training, aerobic exercises, walking, or yoga, may also be considered to improve mental health and work capacity. 4. Targeted Interventions for Health, Humanitarian, and Emergency Workers: Psychosocial interventions aimed at stress management and self-care, or training in communication skills, should be made available to workers experiencing emotional distress. Mindfulness-based or cognitive-behavioral approaches, as well as problem-solving training, may be considered to reduce symptoms of emotional distress and improve work effectiveness. Physical exercise, such as aerobic training or weight training, may also be beneficial for reducing symptoms of emotional distress. 5. Support for Returning to Work After Mental Health-Related Absences: For individuals returning to work after an absence due to mental health conditions, the following approaches should be considered: A combination of work-directed care and evidence-based clinical mental health care. Evidence-based clinical mental health care alone. These interventions aim to reduce mental health symptoms and minimize the number of days absent from work. The WHO guidelines aim to facilitate actions at both national and workplace levels in policy development, service planning, and delivery within the domains of mental and occupational health. By implementing these evidence-based interventions, the guidelines seek to improve mental health outcomes and promote a healthier, more productive workforce.
